questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which process do green plants use to make their own food with the help of sunlight?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis is the process in which green plants use sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to make food.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which green pigment in leaves traps the energy of sunlight?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in leaves that captures sunlight for photosynthesis.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which two raw materials does a leaf need for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air through stomata, and water comes up from the roots.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A potted plant is kept in a dark cupboard for several days. A leaf from it is then tested with iodine solution and does not turn blue-black. Explain why.
questions.answer: Without light the leaf cannot carry out photosynthesis, so it makes no starch. The starch it had before has been used up. Iodine turns blue-black only in the presence of starch.
keyPoints: No light means no photosynthesis
No starch is present
Iodine turns blue-black only with starch
questions.explanation: Iodine is a test for starch, which is made in leaves only when photosynthesis is going on.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Cuscuta (amarbel) is a yellow, thread-like plant without chlorophyll. How does it get its food?
options: It feeds on dead and rotting matter
It takes ready-made food from the host plant it climbs on
questions.explanation: Cuscuta is a parasite that absorbs food from the plant on which it grows.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The pitcher plant has green leaves and makes food by photosynthesis, yet it also traps insects. What is the most likely reason?
options: It grows in soil poor in nitrogen and gets this nutrient from the insects
It cannot take in carbon dioxide
It has no roots at all
It cannot make food in sunlight
questions.explanation: Insectivorous plants such as the pitcher plant grow in nitrogen-poor soil and digest insects to get nitrogen.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Animals and plants both use oxygen all the time. Explain why the amount of oxygen in the air does not run out.
questions.answer: Green plants release oxygen during photosynthesis in the daytime. This replaces the oxygen used up in respiration by living things, so the oxygen content of air stays almost steady.
keyPoints: Photosynthesis releases oxygen
Oxygen used in respiration is replaced
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis adds oxygen to the air while respiration and burning remove it, keeping a balance.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which gas is given out by green plants during photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is released as a by-product of photosynthesis.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In which part of the human digestive system does digestion of food begin?
questions.explanation: Food is chewed in the mouth and saliva starts acting on starch there.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which organ makes bile juice?
questions.explanation: The liver makes bile, which helps in the digestion of fats.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Where is most of the digested food absorbed into the blood?
questions.explanation: The inner wall of the small intestine has villi that absorb digested food into the blood.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What are villi and what is their use in the small intestine?
questions.answer: Villi are finger-like projections on the inner wall of the small intestine. They increase the surface area so that digested food can be absorbed into the blood more quickly.
keyPoints: Finger-like projections in the small intestine
Increase surface area for absorption
questions.explanation: A larger surface area allows more digested food to be absorbed in less time.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these animals chews the cud?
questions.explanation: A cow swallows grass quickly and later brings it back to the mouth to chew again as cud.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How does an amoeba take in food?
options: By absorbing it through its gills
By engulfing it with finger-like false feet called pseudopodia
By filtering it with its teeth
questions.explanation: An amoeba surrounds a food particle with pseudopodia and takes it into a food vacuole.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A cow can live on grass but a human cannot. Which is the correct reason?
options: Grass has no nutrients for humans because it is green
A cow has bacteria in a large caecum that help break down cellulose
questions.explanation: Grass is rich in cellulose, which the cow can digest with the help of bacteria in its large caecum.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A student says food is digested only in the stomach. Using the mouth and small intestine as examples, show that this is not correct.
questions.answer: Digestion starts in the mouth, where saliva begins to break down starch. Digestion is completed in the small intestine, where juices from the liver, pancreas and the intestine itself act on carbohydrates, proteins and fats. So several organs take part.
keyPoints: Saliva acts on starch in the mouth
Digestion is completed in the small intestine
Several organs and juices are involved
questions.explanation: Digestion happens in many parts of the alimentary canal, not only in the stomach.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the removal of the fleece of a sheep called?
questions.explanation: Shearing is the process of cutting the fleece from the sheep's body.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Silk fibres are obtained from the cocoon of which animal?
questions.explanation: The silkworm, the larva of the silk moth, spins a cocoon from which silk fibre is obtained.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is sericulture?
questions.answer: Sericulture is the rearing of silkworms for the production of silk.
keyPoints: Rearing of silkworms
Done to obtain silk
questions.explanation: Sericulture is the name for silkworm rearing and silk production.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: After shearing, the sheep's fleece is washed in tanks to remove grease, dust and dirt. What is this step called?
questions.explanation: Scouring is the washing of sheared wool to clean it.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In which stage of its life cycle does the silk moth spin a cocoon?
questions.explanation: The larva, or caterpillar, spins the cocoon around itself before changing into a pupa.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which animal gives angora wool?
questions.explanation: Angora wool is obtained from the hair of angora goats.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Woollen sweaters keep us warm in winter mainly because:
options: Wool produces heat of its own
The fibres trap air, which is a poor conductor of heat
Wool is a good conductor of heat
Wool stops sunlight from reaching the body
questions.explanation: Air trapped between the wool fibres acts as an insulator and slows heat loss from the body.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Arrange the stages in the life cycle of a silk moth in the correct order.
questions.answer: Egg, then larva (silkworm or caterpillar), then pupa inside the cocoon, then adult moth.
keyPoints: Egg first
Larva then pupa in cocoon
Adult moth last
questions.explanation: The silk moth goes through complete metamorphosis with four stages.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the normal temperature of a healthy human body?
questions.explanation: The normal human body temperature is about 37 degrees Celsius.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: By which mode does heat travel through a solid such as a metal rod?
questions.explanation: In solids, heat is passed from particle to particle by conduction.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Heat from the Sun reaches the Earth by:
questions.explanation: Radiation needs no medium, so heat can cross the empty space between the Sun and the Earth.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why do people prefer to wear light-coloured clothes in summer?
questions.answer: Light-coloured clothes reflect most of the heat falling on them, while dark clothes absorb more heat. So light colours keep us cooler.
keyPoints: Light colours reflect more heat
Dark colours absorb more heat
questions.explanation: Dark surfaces absorb more radiant heat and light surfaces reflect more of it.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which material is the best choice for the handle of a cooking pan?
questions.explanation: Wood is a poor conductor (an insulator) of heat, so the handle stays cool to hold.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Water in a vessel is heated from the bottom. Why does all the water get heated?
options: Heat travels by radiation through the water
Water is a good conductor of heat
Hot water rises and cooler water sinks, setting up convection currents
The vessel makes the water boil on its own
questions.explanation: Heated water becomes lighter and rises while cooler, heavier water comes down, so heat spreads by convection.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why should a clinical thermometer be shaken before use?
options: To bring the mercury thread below the normal mark, because it does not fall back by itself
questions.explanation: A kink near the bulb stops mercury from falling back, so it must be shaken down before the next reading.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: You feel warm when standing a little away from a bonfire even though you are not touching it. Which mode of heat transfer is mainly responsible, and why?
questions.answer: Radiation. Air is a poor conductor, and the warm air mostly rises, so the heat reaching you at the side comes as radiation that travels directly from the fire.
keyPoints: Radiation
Air is a poor conductor
Heat travels without a medium
questions.explanation: Radiation carries heat in all directions without needing contact.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What happens when an acid is put on blue litmus paper?
questions.explanation: Acids turn blue litmus red.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which acid is present in lemon juice?
questions.explanation: Lemon and other citrus fruits contain citric acid.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these turns red litmus paper blue?
questions.explanation: Soap solution is a base, and bases turn red litmus blue.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What are formed when an acid reacts with a base?
questions.explanation: Neutralisation of an acid by a base gives a salt and water.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is baking soda or calamine solution rubbed on the skin after an ant bite?
questions.answer: An ant sting injects formic acid. Baking soda or calamine is a base, so it neutralises the acid and soothes the skin.
keyPoints: Ant sting contains formic acid
Base neutralises the acid
questions.explanation: A base cancels the effect of the acid in a neutralisation reaction.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A turmeric stain on a white shirt turns reddish when rubbed with soap. What does this show?
options: Soap is a base and turmeric turns red with bases
questions.explanation: Turmeric is a natural indicator that turns red in a basic solution such as soap.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A solution does not change the colour of either red or blue litmus paper. The solution is:
questions.explanation: A neutral solution, like sugar solution or common salt solution, gives no change with litmus.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A farmer finds that the soil in a field is too acidic for crops. What can be added to it and why?
questions.answer: Slaked lime or quicklime can be added. These are bases, so they neutralise the extra acid in the soil and make it more suitable for crops.
keyPoints: Add a base such as slaked lime or quicklime
It neutralises the acid in soil
questions.explanation: Neutralisation with a base reduces the acidity of soil.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which acid is responsible for the pain of an ant sting?
questions.explanation: Ants inject formic acid when they sting.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these is a physical change?
questions.explanation: Melting only changes the state of water; no new substance forms.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
questions.explanation: Rust is a new substance, so rusting is a chemical change.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which two things are needed for iron to rust?
questions.explanation: Iron rusts when it is in contact with oxygen and moisture.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which gas turns lime water milky?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with lime water to make it milky.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State two differences between a physical change and a chemical change.
questions.answer: In a physical change no new substance is formed and the change can usually be reversed, like melting wax. In a chemical change one or more new substances are formed and the change is generally not easily reversed, like burning wood.
keyPoints: Physical change forms no new substance
Chemical change forms a new substance
Physical changes are usually reversible
questions.explanation: The main test is whether a new substance with new properties is made.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A candle is burning. Which statement is correct?
options: Both melting of wax and burning are chemical changes
Both melting of wax and burning are physical changes
Melting of wax is a chemical change and burning is a physical change
Melting of wax is a physical change and burning is a chemical change
questions.explanation: Melted wax can solidify again, but burning makes new substances such as carbon dioxide and water vapour.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why are iron gates and railings painted regularly?
options: To keep air and water from reaching the iron and so prevent rusting
To make them dissolve in water
questions.explanation: Paint forms a layer that keeps oxygen and moisture away from the iron.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Vinegar is added to baking soda and bubbles appear. Name the gas, say how you can test for it, and tell whether the change is physical or chemical.
questions.answer: The gas is carbon dioxide. It turns lime water milky. The change is chemical because a new substance (a gas) is formed.
keyPoints: Carbon dioxide is released
It turns lime water milky
A new substance forms so it is chemical
questions.explanation: Gas formation is one sign of a chemical change.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which term describes the average weather pattern of a place over a long period?
questions.explanation: Climate is the average of weather conditions at a place taken over many years.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these animals lives in the polar regions?
questions.explanation: The polar bear is adapted to the very cold Arctic.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which statement about weather and climate is correct?
options: Weather is the average of climate
Weather and climate always mean the same thing
Weather is the day-to-day condition of the atmosphere at a place
questions.explanation: Weather changes from day to day, and climate is its long-term average.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How does a long, strong tail help a monkey living in a tropical rainforest?
options: It helps the monkey grip branches and move among trees
questions.explanation: A long tail helps monkeys hold branches and balance in trees.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is meant by adaptation? Give one example.
questions.answer: Adaptation is a special feature or habit that helps an organism to survive in its surroundings. For example, a polar bear has thick white fur and a layer of fat to stay warm in cold regions.
keyPoints: Feature or habit that helps survival in a habitat
A correct example
questions.explanation: Adaptations match an organism to the conditions where it lives.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How does the white fur of a polar bear help it?
options: It blends with the snow and ice, which helps the bear to hunt without being noticed
It makes the bear sink in water
It attracts the Sun's heat only
questions.explanation: White fur gives camouflage against the snow, and the thick fur also keeps the bear warm.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A news reader says, 'The climate of our city was very hot today.' Is this statement correct? Explain.
questions.answer: No. Climate is the average weather over a long time, so a single hot day is a matter of weather, not climate. The reader should have said the weather was very hot today.
keyPoints: Climate is a long-term average
One day describes weather
questions.explanation: Weather applies to a short time, climate to many years.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these is NOT used to describe the weather of a place?
options: Type of rock in the hills
questions.explanation: Weather is described by temperature, humidity, rainfall and wind speed, not by the type of rock.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is moving air called?
questions.explanation: Air in motion is called wind.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the calm region at the centre of a cyclone called?
questions.explanation: The eye is the calm, clear centre of a cyclone, surrounded by strong winds.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: During the day, near the sea, the breeze blows:
options: From the sky to the sea
questions.explanation: Land warms faster than water, so warm air over land rises and cool air from the sea moves in.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does wind blow? Explain in terms of heated air.
questions.answer: Air that is heated becomes lighter and rises, leaving a region of low pressure. Cooler air from regions of higher pressure moves in to take its place, and this moving air is wind.
keyPoints: Hot air rises
Air moves from high pressure to low pressure
questions.explanation: Differences in air pressure caused by uneven heating produce winds.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: During a thunderstorm with lightning, which is the safest place to be?
options: Inside a closed building or a car
questions.explanation: Lightning tends to strike tall objects and open areas, so a closed building or vehicle is safer.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does the breeze near the coast blow from the land towards the sea at night?
options: There is no air over the land at night
The sea becomes colder than the land
The Sun heats the land at night
The land cools faster than the sea, so the air over the sea is warmer and rises
questions.explanation: At night the warmer air over the sea rises and cooler air from the land moves in to replace it.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why are people living near the coast often moved to cyclone shelters before a cyclone strikes?
questions.answer: A cyclone brings very strong winds, heavy rain and a storm surge that can flood the coast. Moving people to shelters keeps them safe from these dangers.
keyPoints: Strong winds and heavy rain
Flooding from storm surge on the coast
questions.explanation: Early evacuation lowers the loss of life when a cyclone makes landfall.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the process called in which cells release energy from food?
questions.explanation: In cellular respiration, glucose is broken down to release energy.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which organs do fish use to breathe in water?
questions.explanation: Fish take in oxygen dissolved in water through their gills.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Through which openings does a cockroach take in air?
questions.explanation: Insects have tiny openings called spiracles along the sides of the body that lead to air tubes.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What happens to the diaphragm and ribs during inhalation?
options: The diaphragm moves up and the ribs move down
The diaphragm moves down and the ribs move up and outwards
questions.explanation: This increases the space in the chest cavity, so air rushes into the lungs.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is anaerobic respiration? Name one organism that carries it out.
questions.answer: Anaerobic respiration is the breakdown of food to release energy without using oxygen. Yeast is an organism that does this.
keyPoints: Breakdown of food without oxygen
Example such as yeast or bacteria
questions.explanation: Yeast respires anaerobically and gives out alcohol and carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: After running a fast race, a boy gets cramps in his legs. Which substance collecting in the muscles is the usual cause?
questions.explanation: When oxygen is short, muscle cells break glucose down partly, and this produces lactic acid.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does bread dough rise after yeast is added and the dough is kept in a warm place?
questions.answer: Yeast respires and gives out carbon dioxide. The gas gets trapped in the dough as bubbles and makes it swell and rise.
keyPoints: Yeast respires and releases carbon dioxide
Gas bubbles make the dough swell
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide bubbles trapped in dough make bread soft and spongy.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
questions.explanation: The heart pumps blood through blood vessels to all parts of the body.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which red pigment in red blood cells carries oxygen?
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin in red blood cells combines with oxygen and carries it.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In plants, which tissue carries water and minerals from the roots to the leaves?
questions.explanation: Xylem vessels carry water and minerals upwards, while phloem carries food.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which blood vessels carry blood towards the heart?
questions.explanation: Veins bring blood back to the heart, while arteries carry blood away from it.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the function of platelets in the blood?
questions.answer: Platelets help the blood to clot at a wound. The clot stops further bleeding.
keyPoints: Help blood clotting
Stop bleeding from a cut
questions.explanation: Without platelets, even a small cut could keep bleeding.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A balsam stem is placed in water with red ink for some hours. When the stem is cut across, red dots are seen in a ring. What does this show?
options: Food moves down the stem through the xylem
Water moves up the stem through the xylem
The stem makes its own red pigment
Leaves are not needed for water movement
questions.explanation: The coloured water rises through the xylem vessels, which show up as red spots.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is transpiration and why is it useful for a plant?
questions.answer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the leaves through stomata. It helps pull water and minerals upwards from the roots and also cools the plant.
keyPoints: Loss of water vapour through stomata
Helps water rise from the roots
Cools the plant
questions.explanation: Water leaving the leaves creates a pull that draws more water up through the xylem.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which part of a flower is the male reproductive part?
questions.explanation: The stamen, made of the anther and filament, makes pollen.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma called?
questions.explanation: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Bryophyllum can grow new plants from which part?
questions.explanation: Buds at the notches of a Bryophyllum leaf grow into new plantlets.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How are the light, fibrous seeds of a coconut mainly dispersed along the seashore?
questions.explanation: Coconut fruits float on water and are carried by the sea.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Differentiate between pollination and fertilisation in flowers.
questions.answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma. Fertilisation is the joining of the male and female gametes, which happens later inside the ovule.
keyPoints: Pollination is the transfer of pollen
Fertilisation is the fusion of male and female gametes
questions.explanation: Pollination comes first, and fertilisation follows after the pollen tube reaches the ovule.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why do many flowers have bright petals and a sweet scent?
options: To attract insects that help in pollination
questions.explanation: Colour and scent attract insects, which carry pollen from flower to flower.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is it useful for plants to spread their seeds far from the parent plant?
questions.answer: Seeds that fall close to the parent would compete with it for sunlight, water and nutrients. Dispersal reduces this competition and lets the plant grow in new places.
keyPoints: Avoids competition for light, water and nutrients
Helps the species spread to new areas
questions.explanation: Dispersal gives seedlings more room and better chances to survive.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How is speed calculated?
questions.explanation: Speed is the distance covered in unit time.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the SI unit of time?
questions.explanation: The second is the SI unit of time.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which instrument in a vehicle shows its speed at any instant?
questions.explanation: A speedometer shows speed, while the odometer shows the distance travelled.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A bus covers 150 km in 3 hours at a steady speed. What is its speed?
questions.explanation: Speed = 150 km / 3 h = 50 km/h.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A cyclist moves at a steady speed of 5 m/s for 20 seconds. How far does the cyclist travel?
questions.answer: Distance = speed x time = 5 m/s x 20 s = 100 m.
keyPoints: Distance = speed x time
questions.explanation: Multiplying speed by time gives the distance covered.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The distance-time graph of a car is a straight line sloping upwards through the origin. What does it show?
options: The car is moving with a changing speed
The car is moving with a uniform speed
questions.explanation: A straight sloping line means equal distances in equal times, which is uniform speed.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A bus covers 40 km in the first hour and 20 km in the next hour. Find its average speed for the two hours.
questions.answer: Total distance = 40 + 20 = 60 km. Total time = 2 h. Average speed = 60 / 2 = 30 km/h.
keyPoints: Total distance is 60 km
Total time is 2 hours
Average speed is 30 km/h
questions.explanation: Average speed is total distance divided by total time.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which type of material allows electric current to pass through it easily?
questions.explanation: Conductors, such as copper and aluminium, let current flow easily.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the purpose of a fuse in an electric circuit?
options: To protect appliances by breaking the circuit when the current is too high
questions.explanation: The fuse wire melts when too much current passes and cuts off the circuit.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these devices works mainly on the heating effect of current?
questions.explanation: An electric iron has a heating element that becomes hot when current passes through it.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How is a simple electromagnet made?
options: By rubbing a bar with wool
By wrapping insulated wire round an iron core and passing current through it
questions.explanation: Current in the coil magnetises the iron core, and the magnetism stops when the current is switched off.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is the wire used in a fuse made of a metal with a low melting point?
questions.answer: If the current becomes too large, the fuse wire heats up and melts quickly. This breaks the circuit and protects the appliances and wiring from damage.
keyPoints: Wire melts easily when current is too high
Circuit gets broken and appliances are protected
questions.explanation: A fuse is deliberately the weak link of the circuit.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A bulb connected to a fresh cell by wires does not glow, though the bulb is not fused. Which is the most likely reason?
options: The circuit is not complete because of a loose connection
questions.explanation: A bulb glows only when there is a complete closed path for the current.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Give one advantage of an electromagnet over a permanent magnet.
questions.answer: An electromagnet can be switched on and off by turning the current on or off, and its strength can be changed by changing the current or the number of turns of the coil. A permanent magnet cannot be controlled like this.
keyPoints: Can be turned on and off
Strength can be changed
questions.explanation: This is why electromagnets are used in cranes that lift and drop iron scrap.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In which kind of path does light travel in a uniform medium such as air?
questions.explanation: Light travels in straight lines, which is why shadows form.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What does the law of reflection say about the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection?
questions.explanation: The angle of reflection is always equal to the angle of incidence.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which statement about the image formed by a plane mirror is correct?
options: It is smaller than the object
It is real and can be shown on a screen
It is virtual and the same size as the object
questions.explanation: A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image of the same size as the object.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which type of mirror is used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?
questions.explanation: A convex mirror gives a wide field of view and small upright images.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Name the seven colours of white light in order, starting from violet.
questions.answer: Violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red.
keyPoints: Violet, indigo, blue
Green, yellow, orange, red
questions.explanation: White light splits into these seven colours, as seen in a rainbow.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A girl stands 2 m in front of a plane mirror. How far is she from her image?
questions.explanation: The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it, so 2 m + 2 m = 4 m.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why do dentists use a concave mirror to examine teeth?
questions.answer: When a tooth is held close to a concave mirror, the mirror forms a magnified, upright image. This lets the dentist see the tooth clearly in detail.
keyPoints: Concave mirror gives a magnified image of a close object
Image is upright
questions.explanation: A concave mirror enlarges objects placed close to it, within its focal length.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What are the tiny pores on the surface of a leaf, through which gases enter and leave, called?
questions.explanation: Stomata are tiny openings on leaves that allow exchange of gases.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the mode of nutrition called in which an organism makes its own food?
questions.explanation: Autotrophs, like green plants, make their own food.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which bacteria living in the root nodules of pulse plants convert nitrogen of the air into a usable form?
questions.explanation: Rhizobium bacteria fix nitrogen and enrich the soil for leguminous plants.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Mushrooms and bread mould get their food from dead and decaying matter. Such organisms are called:
questions.explanation: Saprotrophs feed on dead and decaying organic matter.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is symbiosis? Give one example from plants.
questions.answer: Symbiosis is a relationship in which two different organisms live together and share shelter and nutrients. In lichens, an alga and a fungus live together; the alga makes food and the fungus gives shelter and holds water.
keyPoints: Two organisms live together and both benefit
Example such as alga and fungus in lichens
questions.explanation: In a symbiotic relationship both partners gain something.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Farmers often grow a pulse crop after a cereal crop in the same field. What is the likely benefit?
options: Pulses remove nitrogen from the soil
Pulses make the soil more acidic
Pulse roots with Rhizobium add nitrogen compounds to the soil
Pulses stop sunlight from reaching the soil
questions.explanation: Rhizobium in pulse roots fixes nitrogen, which improves soil fertility for the next crop.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why do farmers add manure or fertilisers to the soil repeatedly, and which three main nutrients do they supply?
questions.answer: Crops take nutrients from the soil as they grow, so the soil gradually loses them. Manure and fertilisers replace these nutrients; the three main ones are nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
keyPoints: Crops use up soil nutrients
Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium
questions.explanation: Replacing nutrients keeps the soil fertile for the next crop.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In what form do plants store the extra food they make in their leaves?
questions.explanation: Plants store surplus glucose as starch.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many teeth does a healthy adult human usually have?
questions.explanation: An adult normally has 32 permanent teeth.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which type of teeth is used for cutting and biting food?
questions.explanation: Incisors at the front of the mouth cut and bite food.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the main function of the large intestine in digestion?
options: To absorb water from undigested food
questions.explanation: The large intestine takes in water and the remaining waste is passed out as faeces.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which acid is secreted in the stomach and helps to kill harmful germs in food?
questions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills bacteria and helps digestion.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How does food move down the food pipe (oesophagus) to the stomach?
questions.answer: The walls of the food pipe contract and relax in a wave-like movement called peristalsis. This pushes the food down towards the stomach.
keyPoints: Wave-like contraction and relaxation of the muscles
Pushes food towards the stomach
questions.explanation: Peristalsis works along the whole digestive tract.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A child with diarrhoea is given oral rehydration solution (ORS). What is its purpose?
options: To replace the water and salts lost from the body
To stop the child from eating
To kill the bacteria in the stomach
To make the stomach acid stronger
questions.explanation: Diarrhoea causes loss of water and salts, and ORS replaces them.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does the food we eat have to be digested before the body can use it?
questions.answer: Food contains large, insoluble molecules which cannot pass through the walls of the intestine into the blood. Digestion breaks them into small, soluble substances that can be absorbed and carried to the cells.
keyPoints: Large insoluble food molecules cannot be absorbed
Digestion changes them to small soluble substances
questions.explanation: Only small dissolved substances can pass into the blood.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the removal of undigested food from the body through the anus called?
questions.explanation: Egestion is the removal of undigested waste as faeces.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Silkworms are fed on the leaves of which plant?
questions.explanation: Silkworms feed on mulberry leaves.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these animals gives wool?
questions.explanation: Yak hair is used for wool in places like Tibet and Ladakh.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: After scouring, small fluffy fibres stuck to the hair are picked out. What are these fibres called?
questions.explanation: These small fibres are called burrs and are removed before the wool is spun.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the process of making yarn from fibres called?
questions.explanation: Fibres are twisted together in spinning to make yarn.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is done during the sorting of sheared wool?
questions.answer: The sheared fleece is sorted into groups according to the texture and quality of the hair. This is done by hand in the factory so that wool of one type is processed together.
keyPoints: Wool is grouped by texture or type
Done before further processing
questions.explanation: Sorting is one step between shearing and spinning of wool.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why are silkworm cocoons usually processed before the moth comes out?
options: The moth would break the continuous thread of silk as it emerges
The moth turns the silk white
questions.explanation: A long unbroken silk thread is wanted, and an emerging moth would cut it.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Name two animals other than a sheep that give us wool or wool-like fibre, and name the fibre or wool for one of them.
questions.answer: Goats and yaks both give wool. The angora goat gives angora wool, and the Kashmiri goat gives the fine wool used in shawls. Camels, llamas and alpacas also give wool.
keyPoints: Two correct animals such as goat, yak, camel
A correct wool or fibre name
questions.explanation: Hair of several animals, not just sheep, is used to make wool.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: At what temperature does pure water boil at normal atmospheric pressure?
questions.explanation: Pure water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the usual unit in which we measure temperature in daily life in India?
questions.explanation: Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the range of a clinical thermometer?
questions.explanation: A clinical thermometer reads from about 35 degrees C to 42 degrees C.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: When a hot object touches a cold object, in which direction does heat flow?
options: From the cold object to the hot object
From the hot object to the cold object
In both directions equally for ever
questions.explanation: Heat always flows from a hotter body to a colder body.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the difference between a conductor and an insulator of heat? Give two examples of each.
questions.answer: A conductor allows heat to pass through it easily, such as copper and iron. An insulator does not allow heat to pass easily, such as wood and plastic.
keyPoints: Conductors pass heat easily, with examples like metals
Insulators do not, with examples like wood or plastic
questions.explanation: Metals are good conductors and most non-metals are insulators.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: On a cold morning an iron chair feels colder than a wooden stool kept in the same room. Why?
options: Wood absorbs heat from the room
Iron conducts heat away from the hand faster than wood does
questions.explanation: Both are at room temperature; iron simply takes heat from the hand faster, so it feels colder.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does a vacuum flask keep hot tea hot for a long time?
questions.answer: A flask has two walls with a vacuum between them, which stops heat passing by conduction and convection. The shiny surfaces reflect heat back, which cuts down radiation, and the stopper prevents loss of heat through the opening.
keyPoints: Vacuum between double walls reduces conduction and convection
Shiny surfaces reduce radiation
questions.explanation: A flask is built to reduce all three modes of heat transfer.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which acid is present in vinegar?
questions.explanation: Vinegar contains acetic acid.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: From which natural source is litmus obtained?
questions.explanation: Litmus is obtained from lichens.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is milk of magnesia taken for indigestion caused by too much acid in the stomach?
options: It is an acid that adds to the stomach acid
It is a neutral liquid that dilutes the food
It is a base that neutralises the excess acid
It makes the stomach produce more juice
questions.explanation: Milk of magnesia is a base and neutralises the excess stomach acid.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A piece of china rose petals in water is used as an indicator. What colour does the solution become when an acid is added?
questions.explanation: China rose indicator turns acidic solutions dark pink or magenta and basic solutions green.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is an indicator? Name two natural indicators.
questions.answer: An indicator is a substance that shows by a change in colour whether a solution is acidic, basic or neutral. Litmus and turmeric are natural indicators, and so is china rose.
keyPoints: Shows a colour change in acid or base
Two examples such as litmus, turmeric, china rose
questions.explanation: Indicators help us test the nature of a substance.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: When hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide, which products are formed?
questions.explanation: Acid + base gives a salt (sodium chloride) and water in neutralisation.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which group lists only substances that are acidic in nature?
options: Soap solution, lime water, baking soda
Vinegar, soap solution, milk of magnesia
questions.explanation: Vinegar, lemon juice and curd contain acetic, citric and lactic acids respectively.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why should acidic waste from factories be neutralised before it is let into a river?
questions.answer: Acidic waste harms fish and other water life. Adding a base neutralises the acid so that the water becomes safe for living things.
keyPoints: Acid harms aquatic life
A base neutralises the acid
questions.explanation: Neutralisation reduces the harm of chemical waste to the environment.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
questions.explanation: Cooking forms new substances in the food.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Dissolving sugar in water is an example of:
questions.explanation: Sugar can be recovered by evaporating the water, so no new substance is formed.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A magnesium ribbon burns in air with a dazzling white flame. What is the white powder left behind?
questions.explanation: Magnesium combines with oxygen of the air to form magnesium oxide.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the coating of zinc on iron to protect it from rusting called?
questions.explanation: Galvanisation covers iron with a layer of zinc.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is crystallisation? How can crystals of copper sulphate be obtained from its solution?
questions.answer: Crystallisation is the process of getting crystals of a pure substance from its solution. A hot, saturated solution of copper sulphate is cooled slowly without disturbing it, and blue crystals form.
keyPoints: Process of forming crystals from a solution
Cooling a saturated solution slowly
questions.explanation: Crystallisation is a physical change because the same substance is recovered.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: An iron nail is dipped in copper sulphate solution. After some time the blue colour of the solution fades and the nail gets a brownish coating. What does this show?
options: A chemical change happened because a new substance, copper, formed
questions.explanation: The change of colour and the new brown deposit of copper show a chemical reaction.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Classify each as a physical or a chemical change: (a) making ice from water, (b) burning of coal, (c) souring of milk.
questions.answer: (a) Physical change. (b) Chemical change. (c) Chemical change.
keyPoints: Ice making is physical
Burning coal and souring of milk are chemical
questions.explanation: Burning and souring make new substances, while freezing only changes the state of water.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which instrument is used to measure the amount of rainfall?
questions.explanation: A rain gauge collects and measures rain.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What does humidity mean?
options: Amount of water vapour in the air
questions.explanation: Humidity is the moisture, or water vapour, in the air.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which describes the climate of a tropical rainforest?
options: Hot and humid with heavy rainfall
Hot and dry with almost no rain
questions.explanation: Rainforests near the equator are warm and wet through the year.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: On which continent do penguins live in the wild near the South Pole?
questions.explanation: Penguins are found in Antarctica and some other southern regions.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why do some birds migrate to other places at certain times of the year?
questions.answer: They move to escape very cold or harsh weather and to find food and a suitable place to breed. They return when conditions improve.
keyPoints: To escape harsh weather
To find food or a place to breed
questions.explanation: Migration is a way of adapting to seasonal change.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why do polar animals such as seals and penguins have a thick layer of fat under the skin?
options: It helps them dig in the sand
It makes them look bigger to predators only
It acts as insulation and keeps body heat in
questions.explanation: Fat insulates the body and reduces heat loss in cold water and air.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is it much hotter near the equator than near the poles?
questions.answer: Near the equator the Sun's rays fall almost straight down, so a small area gets a lot of heat. Near the poles the rays fall at a slant and the same energy spreads over a larger area, so it is colder.
keyPoints: Rays are nearly vertical at the equator
Rays are slanting at the poles and spread over a larger area
questions.explanation: The angle at which sunlight falls decides how much it heats the surface.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which instrument measures wind speed?
questions.explanation: An anemometer measures the speed of wind.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What happens to air when it is heated?
questions.explanation: Hot air expands, becomes less dense and rises.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Over which part of the earth do tropical cyclones form?
questions.explanation: Tropical cyclones form over warm ocean waters in the tropics.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is a funnel-shaped column of rapidly spinning air that reaches from a cloud to the ground called?
questions.explanation: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air touching the ground.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is a lightning conductor fitted on tall buildings?
questions.answer: A lightning conductor gives lightning an easy path to the ground through a thick metal strip. This protects the building and the people inside from the electric discharge.
keyPoints: Gives lightning a path to the ground
Protects the building
questions.explanation: The conductor carries the huge current safely to the earth.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The air pressure at place X is higher than at place Y. In which direction will the wind blow?
questions.explanation: Air moves from a region of high pressure to a region of low pressure.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Write two precautions to be taken during a thunderstorm.
questions.answer: Stay inside a building or car and keep away from windows. Do not stand under a tall tree or in open fields, and avoid using electrical appliances or water taps.
keyPoints: Stay indoors or in a closed vehicle
Avoid tall trees, open spaces and electric appliances
questions.explanation: Lightning is attracted to tall objects, and metal pipes and wires can carry current.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which gas do we take in from the air for respiration?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is used in cells to release energy from food.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A frog breathes through its lungs and through its:
questions.explanation: A frog can take in oxygen through its moist skin as well as lungs.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: An earthworm takes in oxygen through its:
questions.explanation: An earthworm breathes through its moist skin.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which solution can be used to show that exhaled air has more carbon dioxide than inhaled air?
questions.explanation: Lime water turns milky more quickly with exhaled air.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does the breathing rate of a person go up during exercise?
questions.answer: The muscles work harder and need more energy, so the cells need more oxygen to break down glucose. Breathing faster brings in more oxygen and removes the extra carbon dioxide.
keyPoints: Muscles need more energy
More oxygen is needed and more carbon dioxide has to be removed
questions.explanation: Breathing rate matches the energy demand of the body.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Plants in a pot are watered so much that the soil stays flooded for many days and the roots begin to die. What is the most likely reason?
options: Roots cannot get enough air from the soil for respiration
Roots cannot absorb water at all
questions.explanation: Roots respire using air in the spaces between soil particles, and water fills these spaces.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Explain the difference between breathing and respiration.
questions.answer: Breathing is the taking in of oxygen-rich air and giving out of carbon dioxide-rich air by the body. Respiration is the process inside cells in which glucose is broken down with oxygen to release energy.
keyPoints: Breathing is the exchange of air
Respiration releases energy from food in cells
questions.explanation: Breathing supplies oxygen for respiration in the cells.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the liquid part of the blood called?
questions.explanation: Plasma is the pale yellow liquid in which blood cells float.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which blood cells help to fight germs that enter the body?
questions.explanation: White blood cells protect the body against disease-causing germs.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which organ filters waste from the blood and forms urine?
questions.explanation: The kidneys remove waste and extra water from the blood as urine.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which structures of a plant absorb water from the soil?
questions.explanation: Root hairs have a large surface area and absorb water and minerals.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State one difference between xylem and phloem.
questions.answer: Xylem carries water and minerals from the roots to the leaves. Phloem carries the food made in the leaves to the other parts of the plant.
keyPoints: Xylem carries water and minerals
Phloem carries food
questions.explanation: Both are vascular tissues but they carry different materials.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why do arteries have thick, muscular walls?
options: Because they carry blood back to the heart slowly
Because they carry blood away from the heart at high pressure
Because they exchange gases with cells
questions.explanation: Blood pumped out of the heart is under high pressure, so artery walls are thick and elastic.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why do capillaries have very thin walls?
questions.answer: Capillaries are where oxygen, nutrients and waste are exchanged between the blood and the body cells. Thin walls let these substances pass through easily.
keyPoints: Exchange between blood and cells happens here
Thin walls allow easy passage
questions.explanation: Capillaries connect arteries to veins and are the site of exchange.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
questions.explanation: The human heart has four chambers: two upper atria and two lower ventricles.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which part of a flower is the female reproductive part?
questions.explanation: The pistil, made of stigma, style and ovary, is the female part.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which part of the flower develops into the fruit?
questions.explanation: After fertilisation the ovary grows into the fruit.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Yeast reproduces asexually by:
questions.explanation: A small bulge or bud grows on the yeast cell and separates to form a new cell.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these plants reproduces by means of spores?
questions.explanation: Ferns and mosses produce tiny spores that grow into new plants.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is vegetative propagation? Give two examples of plants grown this way.
questions.answer: Vegetative propagation is the growth of new plants from a vegetative part such as a stem, root or leaf, without using seeds. Rose is grown from stem cuttings and potato grows from its buds (eyes).
keyPoints: New plants from stem, root or leaf
Two correct examples
questions.explanation: It is a form of asexual reproduction.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Fruits of the Xanthium plant have hooks. How does this feature help the plant?
options: The hooks stick to the fur of animals and carry the seeds far away
The hooks help the fruit float
The hooks make the fruit burst
The hooks help to attract bees
questions.explanation: Hooked or spiny fruits cling to animals and are dispersed over long distances.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A gardener plants cuttings from a rose bush that has deep red flowers. Why will the new plants also have deep red flowers?
questions.answer: Plants grown from cuttings come from a single parent by vegetative propagation. They have the same characters as the parent, so they bear flowers of the same colour.
keyPoints: Only one parent is involved
Offspring are identical to the parent
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction produces offspring identical to the parent.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The to-and-fro motion of the bob of a pendulum is an example of which kind of motion?
questions.explanation: A pendulum repeats its motion after equal intervals of time, which is periodic motion.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What do we call the time taken by a pendulum to complete one oscillation?
questions.explanation: The time for one complete oscillation is called the time period.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A car moving along a straight road shows which kind of motion?
questions.explanation: Motion along a straight line is called rectilinear motion.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How long will a vehicle moving at a steady 60 km/h take to cover 120 km?
questions.explanation: Time = distance / speed = 120 / 60 = 2 hours.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the difference between uniform and non-uniform motion? Give one example of each.
questions.answer: In uniform motion a body covers equal distances in equal intervals of time, like a car moving at a constant speed on a straight road. In non-uniform motion it covers unequal distances in equal intervals of time, like a bus in city traffic.
keyPoints: Uniform motion has equal distances in equal times
Non-uniform motion has unequal distances in equal times
questions.explanation: Constant speed means uniform motion, and changing speed means non-uniform motion.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is a speed of 72 km/h in metres per second?

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A simple pendulum completes 20 oscillations in 40 seconds. What is its time period?
questions.answer: Time period = total time / number of oscillations = 40 / 20 = 2 seconds.
keyPoints: Divide total time by number of oscillations
The answer is 2 s
questions.explanation: Each oscillation takes 40 / 20 = 2 seconds.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the use of a switch in an electric circuit?
options: To open or close the circuit
questions.explanation: A switch breaks or completes the circuit.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these is a source of electric current for a torch?
questions.explanation: A cell supplies the electric energy to push current round the circuit.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In the symbol of an electric cell, which line represents the positive terminal?
questions.explanation: The longer line is the positive terminal and the shorter thick line is the negative terminal.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Who discovered that an electric current flowing in a wire deflects a magnetic compass needle placed near it?
questions.explanation: Oersted observed this in 1820 and showed the magnetic effect of current.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the difference between an open circuit and a closed circuit?
questions.answer: In a closed circuit there is a complete unbroken path, so current flows and the bulb glows. In an open circuit the path is broken, for example by an open switch, so no current flows.
keyPoints: Closed circuit has a complete path and current flows
Open circuit has a break and no current flows
questions.explanation: Current needs a continuous conducting path from one terminal of the cell to the other.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is the filament of an electric bulb made of tungsten?
options: Tungsten has a very high melting point and can glow without melting
questions.explanation: The filament becomes white hot, so it must be a metal with a very high melting point.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why should electrical appliances never be handled with wet hands?
questions.answer: Water, especially if it has salts in it, can conduct electricity. With wet hands, current may pass through the body and cause a dangerous electric shock.
keyPoints: Water conducts electricity
Current can flow through the body and cause a shock
questions.explanation: Dry insulating conditions protect us from electric shock.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A material that allows light to pass through it completely so that objects behind are clearly seen is called:
questions.explanation: Clear glass and water are transparent materials.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A rainbow is formed because of which process?
options: Dispersion of sunlight by water drops
questions.explanation: Water droplets in the air split sunlight into its seven colours.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which kind of lens is used in a magnifying glass?
questions.explanation: A convex lens, thicker at the middle, forms an enlarged image when the object is close.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: When is a shadow formed?
options: When an opaque object blocks the path of light
When there is no light source
questions.explanation: An opaque object stops light, leaving a dark region behind it.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is the word AMBULANCE written in reversed letters on the front of the vehicle?
questions.answer: A driver ahead sees the word in the rear-view mirror. A mirror shows lateral inversion, which swaps left and right, so the reversed word looks normal and can be read easily.
keyPoints: Mirror image is laterally inverted
Reversed writing is read correctly in a mirror
questions.explanation: Lateral inversion in a mirror reverses the word a second time.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A rough wall reflects light but we do not see our image in it. Why?
options: The wall is a transparent material
Light does not reach the wall
Light is scattered in many directions, so there is diffuse reflection
questions.explanation: A rough surface reflects parallel rays in different directions, so no clear image forms.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How does a convex lens differ from a concave lens in shape and in the way it affects parallel rays of light?
questions.answer: A convex lens is thicker in the middle and bends parallel rays so that they come together (converge). A concave lens is thinner in the middle and spreads the rays apart (diverges).
keyPoints: Convex is thicker in the middle and converges light
Concave is thinner in the middle and diverges light
questions.explanation: The shape decides whether the lens gathers or spreads the light.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which part of a plant is the main food-making organ?
questions.explanation: Leaves contain chlorophyll and are where most photosynthesis takes place.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which source of energy is needed for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Sunlight provides the energy that chlorophyll uses to make food.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these is an insectivorous plant?
questions.explanation: The Venus flytrap traps insects and digests them.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A leaf has green and white patches. After testing with iodine, only the green patches turn blue-black. What does this show?
options: Starch is made in the dark
Iodine is absorbed only by green colour
Chlorophyll is needed to make starch
questions.explanation: Only the green parts, which have chlorophyll, carried out photosynthesis and made starch.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which one of these is a heterotroph?
questions.explanation: A mushroom has no chlorophyll and depends on other organisms for food.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide + water, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, gives glucose (food) + oxygen.
keyPoints: Carbon dioxide and water are the raw materials
Glucose and oxygen are the products
Sunlight and chlorophyll are needed
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis changes carbon dioxide and water into glucose and releases oxygen.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A strip of black paper is clipped over part of a leaf on a plant kept in sunlight for a few days. When the leaf is tested with iodine, the covered part does not turn blue-black. What is the conclusion?
options: Chlorophyll is absent in the covered part
Light is needed for the formation of starch
Water cannot reach the covered part
Carbon dioxide is made in the covered part
questions.explanation: The only difference between the two parts is light, so light is needed for starch formation.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How does a parasitic plant differ from a saprotroph in the way it gets food? Give an example of each.
questions.answer: A parasite takes food from the body of a living host plant; Cuscuta is an example. A saprotroph takes food from dead and decaying matter; a mushroom is an example.
keyPoints: Parasite feeds on a living host
Saprotroph feeds on dead or decaying matter
One correct example of each
questions.explanation: Both depend on others for food, but one uses living and the other dead organisms.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Saliva in the mouth acts on which nutrient in food?
questions.explanation: Saliva turns starch into sugar.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Where is the bile juice made by the liver stored until it is needed?
questions.explanation: The gall bladder stores bile.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many milk teeth do children usually have?
questions.explanation: A child has 20 milk teeth, which are later replaced by permanent teeth.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In which organ is food churned with digestive juices to form a semi-liquid mixture?
questions.explanation: The muscular walls of the stomach churn food while it mixes with the gastric juices.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The pancreatic juice acts on which nutrients?
questions.explanation: The pancreas makes a juice that digests carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the role of bile juice in digestion?
questions.answer: Bile breaks fats into very tiny droplets, which makes it easier for the enzymes to digest them. It is made by the liver and poured into the small intestine.
keyPoints: Acts on fats
Made by the liver and released into the small intestine
questions.explanation: Bile helps digest fats.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Grass-eating animals such as cattle have a longer small intestine than meat-eating animals such as lions. What is the best reason?
options: Plant food is bulky and harder to digest, so it takes longer to digest and absorb
questions.explanation: Cellulose-rich plant food needs more time and a longer path for digestion.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Describe the path taken by a piece of bread from the mouth until the undigested part leaves the body.
questions.answer: Bread goes from the mouth down the food pipe to the stomach, then to the small intestine, then to the large intestine, and the undigested waste leaves through the anus.
keyPoints: Mouth, food pipe, stomach
Small intestine, large intestine, anus
questions.explanation: These organs together make up the alimentary canal.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The pointed teeth in the human mouth used for tearing food are called:
questions.explanation: Canines are pointed and tear food.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Wool is obtained from which part of a sheep?
questions.explanation: Wool is the hair (fleece) of a sheep.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is a cocoon?
questions.answer: A cocoon is the protective covering of silk thread that the silkworm spins around itself before it becomes a moth.
keyPoints: A covering of silk thread
Spun by the silkworm before it turns into a moth
questions.explanation: Silk fibre is obtained from cocoons.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these fibres comes from an animal?
questions.explanation: Silk is an animal fibre, while cotton and jute are plant fibres.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What do we call the process of taking out silk threads from cocoons?
questions.explanation: In reeling, silk threads are unwound from the cocoons.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Wool and silk are both fibres made mostly of:
questions.explanation: Both wool and silk are protein fibres.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Name any three steps in the processing of fleece into wool in the correct order, after shearing.
questions.answer: After shearing, the fleece is scoured (washed), then sorted by quality, then the burrs are picked out. Later the fibres are dyed and spun into yarn.
keyPoints: Scouring comes first
Sorting and removing burrs follow
Dyeing and spinning come later
questions.explanation: Raw fleece is cleaned and sorted before it can be spun.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Shearing does not hurt the sheep. What is the best reason?
options: Sheep have no feeling in their skin
Only the outer hair is cut, like a haircut, and the skin is not harmed
The sheep is made to sleep
questions.explanation: Shearing removes the hair and not the skin, and the hair grows back.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Compare the sources of wool and silk.
questions.answer: Wool comes from the fleece or hair of animals such as sheep, goat and yak. Silk comes from the cocoon spun by the silkworm, which is the larva of the silk moth.
keyPoints: Wool from hair of animals like sheep, goat, yak
Silk from the cocoon of the silkworm
questions.explanation: Both are animal fibres but they come from different parts and animals.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: By which mode does heat mainly travel in liquids and gases?
questions.explanation: Liquids and gases transfer heat by the movement of the heated material, which is convection.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which one of these is a good conductor of heat?
questions.explanation: Metals like copper are good conductors.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the range of a laboratory thermometer?
questions.explanation: A laboratory thermometer typically measures from -10 degrees C to 110 degrees C.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: While measuring the temperature of hot water with a laboratory thermometer, how should the bulb be placed?
options: Touching the bottom of the beaker
Fully in the water without touching the bottom or sides
Touching the side of the beaker
questions.explanation: Touching the bottom or sides would give the temperature of the glass, which may be hotter than the water.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is conduction of heat? Give an example.
questions.answer: Conduction is the transfer of heat through a substance from the hot part to the cooler part without the substance itself moving. For example, the handle of a metal spoon becomes hot when the other end is in hot tea.
keyPoints: Heat passes from particle to particle
A correct example
questions.explanation: Conduction mainly takes place in solids.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why are dark-coloured clothes preferred in winter, if one wants to stay warm in the sunshine?
options: Dark colours absorb more heat from the Sun
questions.explanation: Dark surfaces absorb more heat radiation than light surfaces.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why do cooking vessels often have a copper or aluminium base?
questions.answer: Copper and aluminium are good conductors of heat. They quickly pass the heat from the flame to the food inside, so cooking is faster.
keyPoints: Copper and aluminium are good conductors
Heat passes quickly to the food
questions.explanation: Good conductors transfer heat rapidly from the flame to the contents.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these substances is basic in nature?
questions.explanation: Baking soda solution is basic and turns red litmus blue.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which acid is found in tamarind?
questions.explanation: Tamarind contains tartaric acid.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which natural indicator changes from yellow to red in a basic solution?
questions.explanation: Turmeric turns red with bases such as soap solution.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which acid is present in curd and sour milk?
questions.explanation: Lactic acid is formed in milk when it sours or turns to curd.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What taste and feel are generally typical of bases?
options: Bitter and soapy to the touch
questions.explanation: Bases taste bitter and feel soapy, though one should never taste unknown chemicals.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is neutralisation? Give an example.
questions.answer: Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base in which both lose their properties and form a salt and water. For example, hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide gives sodium chloride and water.
keyPoints: Acid reacts with base
Salt and water are formed
questions.explanation: Neutralisation cancels the acidic and basic nature of the two substances.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A curry stain on a white shirt turns red when rubbed with soap but fades back to yellowish when the shirt is rinsed well with water. Why?
options: Turmeric changes colour in soap, and rinsing removes the soap, so the yellow returns
Water is an acid that makes the stain disappear
questions.explanation: Soap, a base, turns turmeric red; when the soap is washed out, the red colour is gone.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: You have three unlabelled colourless solutions: an acid, a base and a neutral solution. How can red and blue litmus papers be used to tell them apart?
questions.answer: Dip both a red and a blue litmus paper in each solution. The one that turns blue litmus red is the acid. The one that turns red litmus blue is the base. The one that changes neither is neutral.
keyPoints: Acid turns blue litmus red
Base turns red litmus blue
Neutral solution changes neither
questions.explanation: Litmus shows both acidic and basic nature.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Tearing a sheet of paper into small pieces is which kind of change?
questions.explanation: The pieces are still paper, so no new substance is formed.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the reddish-brown coating that forms on iron objects left in moist air called?
questions.explanation: Rust is the reddish-brown substance formed when iron reacts with oxygen and water.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Stainless steel does not rust easily because it is:
options: Made of iron mixed with carbon and metals like chromium and nickel
questions.explanation: The alloy of iron with chromium, nickel and carbon resists rusting.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which products are formed when a candle burns completely in air?
questions.explanation: Wax contains carbon and hydrogen, which combine with oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water vapour.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Name two things that may be observed during a chemical change.
questions.answer: Examples of what can be observed are a change in colour, release of a gas, production of heat or light, formation of a solid (a precipitate), or a change in smell.
keyPoints: Two correct observations such as colour change, gas, heat, light, precipitate
questions.explanation: These signs tell us that a new substance may be forming.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which one of these is NOT a sure sign of a chemical change?
options: Release of a gas with a new smell
Change in shape of a substance
Change in colour along with release of heat
questions.explanation: A change of shape alone, such as beating a metal into a sheet, can occur in a physical change.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A cut apple turns brown if it is kept in the open for some time. Is this a physical or chemical change? Explain.
questions.answer: It is a chemical change. The cut surface reacts with oxygen of the air and a new brown substance forms, which cannot be changed back to the original.
keyPoints: Chemical change
Reaction with oxygen forms a new substance
questions.explanation: A new substance with a different colour forms, so the change is chemical.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following is a chemical change that takes place in green leaves in sunlight?
questions.explanation: In photosynthesis, carbon dioxide and water change into glucose and oxygen, which are new substances.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which bird with a large colourful beak is found in tropical rainforests?
questions.explanation: The hornbill has a large beak and lives in tropical forests.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Regions lying close to the equator are called:
questions.explanation: The tropical region lies close to the equator and is warm.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The red-eyed tree frog of the rainforest has sticky pads on its feet. What does this help it to do?
options: Climb and cling to leaves and branches
questions.explanation: Sticky pads help the frog hold onto wet leaves and branches.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these describes polar regions?
options: Very cold and covered with ice and snow
questions.explanation: The polar regions near the North and South Poles are icy and very cold.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Write two features that help animals live in the very cold polar regions.
questions.answer: Polar animals have a thick layer of fat under the skin and thick fur or feathers that keep heat in. Some, like the polar bear, are white, which helps them blend in with the snow.
keyPoints: Thick fat layer or fur to keep warm
White colour or another correct feature
questions.explanation: These features reduce heat loss and help with hunting in snow.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which feature helps a penguin move quickly in water?
questions.explanation: Penguins have a streamlined body and flippers that act like paddles.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A forecast says, 'Tomorrow there will be 10 mm of rain in our city.' This statement is about:
questions.explanation: A forecast for one day describes weather, not the long-term average.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why are tropical rainforests home to a very large number of kinds of animals?
questions.answer: The warm and wet climate allows plants to grow all year, so there is plenty of food and shelter. Many different animals can find what they need.
keyPoints: Warm and wet climate throughout the year
Plenty of food and shelter
questions.explanation: Abundant plant growth supports many kinds of animals.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the sound heard after a flash of lightning called?
questions.explanation: Thunder is the sound produced by lightning.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is a cyclone over the north-western Pacific Ocean usually called?
questions.explanation: Tropical cyclones in the north-west Pacific are called typhoons.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these is a sensible preparation when a cyclone warning has been given?
options: Go to the beach to watch
Store drinking water, dry food and a torch
questions.explanation: People should be ready with essentials and move to safe places.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Windmills use the energy of wind to generate electricity. Wind is described as:
options: A source that is used up quickly
questions.explanation: Wind keeps blowing, so it is a renewable source of energy.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Give two uses of wind.
questions.answer: Wind turns windmills to generate electricity or to lift water. It also moves sailing boats, dries clothes and disperses seeds and pollen.
keyPoints: Two correct uses of wind
questions.explanation: Wind energy has been used by people for a very long time.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does a hot-air balloon rise?
options: The hot air inside is heavier than the air outside
The hot air inside is lighter than the cooler air outside
The balloon is filled with water
questions.explanation: Heated air expands and becomes less dense, so the balloon floats up.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: During a thunderstorm we see lightning first and hear thunder a little later. Why?
questions.answer: Lightning and thunder happen at the same moment, but light travels much faster than sound. The light reaches our eyes almost at once, while the sound takes longer to arrive.
keyPoints: Both occur together
Light travels much faster than sound
