questions.explanation: The delay between flash and thunder depends on how far away the lightning is.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which organs are the main organs of breathing in humans?
questions.explanation: Humans breathe with the help of the lungs.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which gas is given out as a waste product of respiration?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is produced and breathed out.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the function of hair and mucus in the nose?
options: To trap dust and germs in the air we breathe in
questions.explanation: Hair and mucus filter the incoming air.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A whale is a sea animal but it breathes with:
options: Lungs, coming to the surface to breathe
questions.explanation: Whales are mammals and have lungs, so they surface to breathe.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
questions.answer: Glucose + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + energy.
keyPoints: Glucose and oxygen react
Carbon dioxide, water and energy are released
questions.explanation: In aerobic respiration, oxygen is used to break down glucose completely.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Yeast is added to a sugar solution and kept warm. Which products form as it respires without oxygen?
questions.explanation: Yeast breaks down sugar to give alcohol and carbon dioxide, a process used in making bread and wine.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why do people who climb to a high mountain often breathe faster?
questions.answer: The air at high altitudes is thin and has less oxygen in each breath. The body breathes faster to try to get enough oxygen.
keyPoints: Less oxygen available at high altitude
Faster breathing takes in more air
questions.explanation: Breathing rate rises to make up for the lower oxygen content of each breath.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What can we feel by placing fingers on the wrist?
questions.explanation: The pulse is the throbbing of an artery caused by the heartbeat.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A person with anaemia has a shortage of:
questions.explanation: In anaemia there is not enough haemoglobin, so less oxygen is carried.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which instrument is used by a doctor to listen to the heartbeat?
questions.explanation: A stethoscope carries the sound of the heartbeat to the doctor's ears.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which tissue of the plant carries food from the leaves to other parts?
questions.explanation: Phloem carries the prepared food from the leaves.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Besides plasma, name the three kinds of components in blood.
questions.answer: Red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
keyPoints: Red blood cells
White blood cells
Platelets
questions.explanation: Plasma carries these cells around the body.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these is a waste product removed by plants?
questions.explanation: Plants store waste in forms such as gums, resins and latex, and also lose it by shedding leaves.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does blood in the veins not flow backwards?
options: Veins have valves that allow flow in one direction
questions.explanation: Valves in veins close to stop blood from flowing backwards.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What would happen to a plant if all the xylem vessels in its stem were blocked?
questions.answer: Water and minerals could not reach the leaves. The leaves could not make food by photosynthesis, so the plant would wilt and eventually die.
keyPoints: Water cannot reach the leaves
No photosynthesis, so the plant wilts and dies
questions.explanation: Xylem is the only way water reaches the leaves.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the process called by which a seed grows into a new plant (seedling)?
questions.explanation: Germination is the sprouting of a seed into a young plant.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In which part of the stamen are the pollen grains made?
questions.explanation: Pollen is produced in the anther.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Pollen falls on the stigma of a flower of another plant of the same kind. This is called:
questions.explanation: Transfer of pollen between flowers of different plants is cross-pollination.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Winged seeds, such as those of the maple, are dispersed mainly by:
questions.explanation: The wings let the seeds drift in the wind.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is fragmentation? Name one plant that reproduces by it.
questions.answer: Fragmentation is a type of asexual reproduction in which the body of an organism breaks into pieces, and each piece grows into a new organism. Spirogyra, an alga, reproduces this way.
keyPoints: Body breaks into pieces that grow into new individuals
Example such as Spirogyra
questions.explanation: Fragmentation is common in simple green algae like Spirogyra.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which part of a potato grows into a new plant?
questions.explanation: Each eye of a potato is a bud that can sprout a new plant.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A flower has stamens but no pistil. Such a flower is called:
questions.explanation: A flower with only the male part is a unisexual male flower.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Put these events in the correct order: seed formation, pollination, fertilisation.
questions.answer: Pollination first, then fertilisation, and finally seed formation.
keyPoints: Pollination comes first
Fertilisation follows
Seeds form last
questions.explanation: Seeds develop from fertilised ovules.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which instrument measures the distance travelled by a vehicle?
questions.explanation: The odometer records the distance covered.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the SI unit of speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is distance divided by time, so its SI unit is metre per second.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: An old device that uses the shadow of a stick to tell the time of day is called a:
questions.explanation: A sundial shows time by the position of the Sun's shadow.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How can you find the speed of a rolling ball using simple instruments?
questions.answer: Measure the distance the ball rolls with a measuring tape and the time it takes with a stopwatch. Then divide the distance by the time to find the speed.
keyPoints: Measure distance with a tape and time with a stopwatch
Speed = distance / time
questions.explanation: Speed needs both distance and time.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: On a distance-time graph, the line for an object is horizontal (parallel to the time axis). What does it show?
options: It is moving with uniform speed
It is moving faster and faster
questions.explanation: The distance does not change with time, so the object is at rest.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which is faster: a cyclist at 10 m/s or a scooter at 30 km/h?
questions.explanation: 10 m/s is 36 km/h, which is greater than 30 km/h.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A car travels 30 km in 30 minutes. Find its speed in km/h.
questions.answer: 30 minutes is 0.5 hour. Speed = 30 km / 0.5 h = 60 km/h.
keyPoints: Convert 30 minutes to 0.5 hour
Speed is 60 km/h
questions.explanation: Units must be consistent before dividing.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these is an insulator of electricity?
questions.explanation: Rubber does not let current flow through it.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A group of two or more cells joined together is called a:
questions.explanation: A battery is made of two or more cells.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which device works on the magnetic effect of electric current?
questions.explanation: An electric bell has an electromagnet that pulls the hammer.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In homes, what do MCBs (miniature circuit breakers) do?
options: They switch off the circuit automatically when the current is too high
questions.explanation: An MCB trips and cuts the current in case of overload, like a fuse but reusable.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Name two electrical appliances that work on the heating effect of electric current.
questions.answer: An electric iron and an electric heater. A geyser or a toaster are also examples.
keyPoints: Two correct appliances such as iron, heater, toaster, geyser
questions.explanation: These appliances have a heating element that gets hot with current.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A fuse in a house circuit has blown. What is the right thing to do?
options: Replace it with a fuse of the correct rating after finding the fault
Replace it with a copper wire
Join the broken ends with a thick wire
Ignore it and keep using the appliance
questions.explanation: A proper fuse of the right rating protects the wiring, and the fault should be checked.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How would you show that a wire carrying a current produces a magnetic effect?
questions.answer: Place a magnetic compass near a straight wire and pass a current through it by closing the switch. The compass needle deflects, showing a magnetic effect of the current. When the switch is opened, the needle returns to its original position.
keyPoints: Compass placed near the wire
Needle deflects when current flows
questions.explanation: This is the experiment that Oersted performed.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these is a luminous object?
questions.explanation: The Sun gives out its own light, so it is luminous; the Moon only reflects sunlight.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Frosted glass lets some light pass but we cannot see clearly through it. It is:
questions.explanation: A translucent material allows only part of the light to pass.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: An image that can be obtained on a screen is called:
questions.explanation: A real image is formed where rays actually meet, so it can be caught on a screen.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which mirror always forms an upright, smaller image of an object?
questions.explanation: A convex mirror forms a diminished, erect, virtual image.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State the two laws of reflection.
questions.answer: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
keyPoints: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection
Incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane
questions.explanation: These laws apply to all reflecting surfaces.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A candle is 10 cm in front of a plane mirror. If it is moved 2 cm closer to the mirror, what will be the distance between the candle and its image?
questions.explanation: The candle is now 8 cm from the mirror, so the image is 8 cm behind it and the distance between them is 16 cm.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is a concave reflector used behind the bulb in a torch or a vehicle headlight?
questions.answer: A concave reflector with the bulb at its focus sends the light out as a parallel beam. This makes the beam strong and directed so that it travels a long way.
keyPoints: Bulb is at the focus
Reflected light forms a parallel beam
questions.explanation: A concave surface can turn light from a point source into a parallel beam.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Chlorophyll is found inside tiny structures in the cells of leaves. What are they called?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: From where do plants absorb mineral salts such as nitrates?
questions.explanation: Roots absorb water and dissolved minerals from the soil.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A water plant like Hydrilla is kept in a funnel under water in sunlight. Bubbles rise from it. Which gas do the bubbles mostly contain?
questions.explanation: The bubbles are oxygen released during photosynthesis.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does Cuscuta look yellow instead of green?
options: It has a lot of chlorophyll
questions.explanation: Cuscuta has no chlorophyll and so depends on its host for food.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Most leaves are thin and flat. How does this help the plant?
questions.answer: A flat, broad leaf has a large surface area to catch sunlight, and it lets carbon dioxide reach the cells easily through the stomata. A thin leaf also lets gases and light reach every cell quickly.
keyPoints: Large surface area to absorb sunlight
Easy entry of carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: The shape of a leaf suits its job of photosynthesis.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: During photosynthesis which change of energy takes place?
options: Light energy becomes chemical energy stored in food
questions.explanation: The energy of sunlight is stored as chemical energy in the food.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is photosynthesis said to be important for almost all living things?
questions.answer: Green plants make food by photosynthesis, and animals, directly or indirectly, depend on plants for food. Photosynthesis also releases the oxygen that most living things need for respiration.
keyPoints: It makes food that all animals depend upon
It releases oxygen
questions.explanation: Plants form the base of nearly every food chain.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the use of the digested food by the cells of the body for growth and repair called?
questions.explanation: Assimilation is the use of absorbed food by body cells.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What are the chemical substances in digestive juices that break down food called?
questions.explanation: Enzymes speed up the breakdown of food into simpler substances.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Into which part of its stomach does a cow first send the quickly swallowed grass?
questions.explanation: Swallowed grass is stored in the rumen, the first chamber, and later brought back as cud.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The stomach wall releases mucus. What is its function?
options: To protect the stomach lining from the acid
questions.explanation: Mucus coats the inner wall of the stomach so that the acid does not harm it.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How does an amoeba digest its food?
questions.answer: The amoeba engulfs food with pseudopodia and encloses it in a food vacuole. Digestive juices act inside the vacuole, the digested food is absorbed, and the undigested part is thrown out through the cell surface.
keyPoints: Food taken into a food vacuole
Digestive juices act and the undigested part is expelled
questions.explanation: An amoeba is a single cell so digestion takes place inside the cell.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: If the liver of a person did not make enough bile, the digestion of which nutrient would be most affected?
questions.explanation: Bile is needed to break fats into small droplets for digestion.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How does chewing the cud help a cow to make use of grass?
questions.answer: The cow swallows grass quickly and stores it in the rumen. Later it brings the partly digested food back to the mouth and chews it again, which breaks the tough fibres into fine pieces that are easier to digest.
keyPoints: Food is brought back from the rumen
Chewing again breaks tough fibres
questions.explanation: Cud chewing helps the digestion of cellulose-rich grass.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In South America, which animals are reared for their wool, alongside sheep?
questions.explanation: Llama and alpaca wool is used in the Andes region.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What hatches from the egg of a silk moth?
questions.explanation: The egg hatches into a larva, also called a silkworm.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In selective breeding of sheep for wool, what do farmers do?
options: Choose parents that have good quality hair and breed them
questions.explanation: Parents with good quality hair are chosen so that lambs also have good wool.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which is a property of silk fibre?
options: It is smooth, shiny and strong
questions.explanation: Silk is a smooth, shiny and strong natural protein fibre.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What do silkworms feed on and what do they do after they have grown fully?
questions.answer: Silkworms feed on mulberry leaves and grow quickly. When fully grown, a silkworm spins a cocoon of silk thread around itself.
keyPoints: Feed on mulberry leaves
Spin a cocoon when fully grown
questions.explanation: The cocoon is made during the larval stage before it becomes a pupa.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which sequence correctly shows the early steps of processing wool?
questions.explanation: The fleece is first sheared, then scoured (cleaned) and then sorted.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the difference between a fibre and a yarn?
questions.answer: A fibre is a very thin, thread-like strand, such as a hair of wool. Yarn is made by twisting many fibres together in spinning, and yarn is used for weaving or knitting cloth.
keyPoints: Fibre is a thin strand
Yarn is made by twisting fibres together
questions.explanation: Fibres are spun into yarn, which is then woven or knitted into fabric.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which liquid metal is often used in thermometers?
questions.explanation: Mercury is used because it expands evenly and is easy to see.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: At what temperature does pure water freeze at normal pressure?
questions.explanation: Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How does a thermometer show a rise in temperature?
options: The liquid in it expands and rises
questions.explanation: On heating, the liquid in the bulb expands and moves up the tube.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why should a clinical thermometer not be used to measure the temperature of boiling water?
options: Its range is only up to about 42 degrees C, so it may break
questions.explanation: A clinical thermometer is designed for the body temperature range and could break at higher temperatures.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is convection? Give one example.
questions.answer: Convection is the transfer of heat in liquids and gases by the movement of the heated material. For example, when water is heated in a pan, the hot water rises and cold water sinks in its place.
keyPoints: Heat transfer by movement of the fluid itself
A correct example such as heating water
questions.explanation: Hot fluid rises and cooler fluid sinks, forming a convection current.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Two thin blankets keep a person warmer than one thick blanket of the same total thickness. What is the reason?
options: Air trapped between the blankets is a poor conductor of heat
questions.explanation: The layer of air between the two blankets acts as an insulator.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A doctor keeps a clinical thermometer in a patient's mouth for about a minute before reading it. Why is this needed?
questions.answer: The mercury has to reach the same temperature as the body and expand to its full level. This takes a little time, so waiting gives the correct reading.
keyPoints: Thermometer must reach body temperature
Mercury needs time to expand fully
questions.explanation: Reading too early would give a lower value than the real body temperature.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these is a mineral acid?
questions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid is made from minerals; the others are found in foods.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the chemical name of common salt?
questions.explanation: Common salt is sodium chloride.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Sodium hydroxide, also called caustic soda, is:
questions.explanation: Sodium hydroxide is a strong base used in making soap.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why should students never taste or touch unknown chemicals in the laboratory?
options: They can be harmful, such as strong acids and bases
questions.explanation: Some acids and bases are corrosive and can harm the skin and body.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: State two properties of acids.
questions.answer: Acids taste sour and turn blue litmus paper red. Some acids, in a strong form, are corrosive and can burn the skin.
keyPoints: Sour taste
Turn blue litmus red
questions.explanation: Foods that taste sour, like lemon and tamarind, contain acids.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A solution turns red litmus blue and turns china rose indicator green. The solution is most likely:
questions.explanation: Both results are typical of a basic solution.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Is common salt acidic, basic or neutral? Name an acid and a base from which it can be made.
questions.answer: Common salt is neutral. It is formed when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide.
keyPoints: Common salt is neutral
Made from hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide
questions.explanation: The salt formed in a complete neutralisation is neutral.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Boiling of water to form steam is:
questions.explanation: Steam is still water, so only the state has changed.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: When a piece of wood burns, ash and gases are formed. This is:
questions.explanation: New substances such as ash and carbon dioxide are formed.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these does NOT help to prevent rusting of iron?
questions.explanation: Water and air cause rusting, so leaving iron in water encourages it.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: When sugar is heated strongly it turns black and gives out fumes. This is because:
options: It melts and the same sugar forms again on cooling
A chemical change happens and new substances form
questions.explanation: Sugar decomposes into carbon (black) and other substances, which cannot be reversed.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is burning a sheet of paper a chemical change?
questions.answer: Burning forms new substances, such as ash, carbon dioxide and water vapour. The paper cannot be recovered from them, so the change is chemical.
keyPoints: New substances form
Paper cannot be recovered
questions.explanation: Irreversible formation of new substances marks a chemical change.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these is a harmful chemical change?
questions.explanation: Rusting damages iron structures, while the others are useful changes.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Three test tubes each hold iron nails: (1) nails in ordinary water open to air, (2) nails in boiled water with a layer of oil on top, (3) nails in dry air. In which tube will rusting occur, and what does this show?
questions.answer: Rusting will take place mainly in tube 1. In tube 2 there is no air (oxygen) reaching the nails, and in tube 3 there is no water. This shows that both air (oxygen) and water are needed for rusting.
keyPoints: Rusting in tube 1
Both oxygen and water are required
questions.explanation: Rust forms only when iron touches both air and moisture.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which instrument is used to measure the temperature of the air?
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these is a polar region of the Earth?
questions.explanation: The Arctic around the North Pole is a polar region.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the main source of energy that drives the weather on Earth?
questions.explanation: Heat from the Sun causes winds, evaporation and rain.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A tiger's coat has dark stripes on a yellowish background. How does this help the tiger in the forest?
options: It makes the tiger look bigger
It makes the tiger run faster
It helps it to blend with tall grass and shadows when hunting
questions.explanation: The stripes help the tiger to hide in vegetation and approach its prey.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is acclimatisation? Give one example.
questions.answer: Acclimatisation is the slow adjustment of a single organism, over days or weeks, to small changes in its surroundings. For example, a mountaineer who stays at high altitude gets used to the thin air.
keyPoints: Gradual adjustment of one organism to a change in its surroundings
A correct example
questions.explanation: Acclimatisation happens within one lifetime and is not inherited.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A person from the plains goes to live in a high mountain area. At first the person gets breathless but after a few weeks feels better. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: The body gradually adjusts to the lower oxygen at high altitude.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How is adaptation different from acclimatisation?
questions.answer: Adaptation is a feature developed by a species over many generations that helps it survive in its habitat. Acclimatisation is a short-term adjustment by one organism to a change in its surroundings.
keyPoints: Adaptation takes place over many generations
Acclimatisation is quick and within one organism
questions.explanation: Adaptation is a long, species-wide process; acclimatisation is individual and short-term.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which instrument measures air pressure?
questions.explanation: A barometer is used to measure atmospheric pressure.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Lightning is a:
options: Large electric discharge in the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Lightning is an electric spark between clouds or between a cloud and the ground.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: As we go higher above the sea level, the air pressure generally:
questions.explanation: There is less air above us at higher altitudes, so the pressure falls.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In sunshine, which gets heated faster?
questions.explanation: Land heats up and cools down faster than water.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why are people advised to unplug electrical appliances and avoid using the telephone line (corded) during a thunderstorm?
questions.answer: Lightning can send a large current through electric wires into the house. This can damage appliances and give a dangerous shock, so it is safer to switch them off and unplug them.
keyPoints: Lightning current can travel through wires
It can damage appliances or shock a person
questions.explanation: Wires can carry lightning-induced current into buildings.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which statement correctly explains a sea breeze during the day?
options: Warm air over the sea rises and air from the land moves in
Warm air over the land rises, the pressure falls, and cooler air from the sea moves in
Cold air rises over the land
questions.explanation: Land is warmer, so air above it rises and creates a low-pressure region that is filled by air from the sea.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does a cyclone become weaker after it moves over land?
questions.answer: A cyclone gets its energy from warm, moist air over the ocean. Over land this supply is cut off, and friction with the ground also slows its winds, so it weakens.
keyPoints: Loses warm moist ocean supply
Friction with land slows the winds
questions.explanation: Cyclones need warm sea water to continue.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Through which tube does air pass to reach the lungs after the nose?
questions.explanation: The windpipe carries air from the throat to the lungs.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the process of breathing out called?
questions.explanation: Exhalation is breathing out.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Through which tiny openings on leaves does a plant take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide for respiration?
questions.explanation: Leaves exchange gases through stomata.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does a fish die if it is taken out of water for a long time?
options: Its gills cannot take in oxygen from air properly
Its lungs are full of water
questions.explanation: Gills are made to take dissolved oxygen from water and dry out in air.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Describe what happens to the diaphragm and ribs when we breathe out.
questions.answer: The ribs move down and inwards and the diaphragm moves up. This reduces the space in the chest cavity, so air is pushed out of the lungs.
keyPoints: Ribs move down and in; diaphragm moves up
Chest space shrinks and air goes out
questions.explanation: Exhalation is the opposite of inhalation.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Fish in a crowded, closed aquarium often come to the water surface. What is the most likely reason?
options: The water has too much oxygen
The water has too little dissolved oxygen
They are looking for food in the air
questions.explanation: Crowding uses up dissolved oxygen, so fish gulp at the surface where oxygen from the air dissolves.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How does smoking harm the lungs?
questions.answer: Tobacco smoke contains tar and other harmful chemicals which damage the lungs and the air passages. This can cause breathing problems, coughing and diseases such as lung cancer.
keyPoints: Smoke contains harmful substances like tar
Damages lungs and causes diseases
questions.explanation: Smoking is a leading cause of lung disease.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which thin blood vessels connect the arteries to the veins?
questions.explanation: Capillaries are very thin vessels where exchange with the cells takes place.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: About how many times does the heart of a healthy adult beat in one minute at rest?
questions.explanation: The usual resting heart rate is about 70 to 80 beats per minute.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which waste substance is found in urine?
questions.explanation: Urea is a nitrogen-containing waste removed in urine.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Besides the kidneys, which organ removes some waste through sweat?
questions.explanation: Sweat glands in the skin remove water and salts with some waste.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the function of the heart?
questions.answer: The heart pumps blood to all parts of the body through blood vessels. The blood carries oxygen and food to cells and removes waste.
keyPoints: Pumps blood
Blood carries oxygen and nutrients and removes wastes
questions.explanation: The heart keeps the blood circulating.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does the heart beat faster during exercise?
options: Muscles need more oxygen and food, so blood must be pumped faster
questions.explanation: Faster circulation delivers more oxygen to working muscles.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Trace the path of oxygen from the lungs to a muscle cell.
questions.answer: Oxygen enters the blood in the lungs and is carried by the haemoglobin in red blood cells. The heart pumps this blood through arteries to capillaries near the muscles, where oxygen passes into the muscle cells.
keyPoints: Oxygen carried by haemoglobin in red blood cells
Heart pumps it through arteries to capillaries and cells
questions.explanation: Blood circulation links the lungs to every body cell.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which outer parts of a flower protect it when it is a bud?
questions.explanation: Sepals are green and enclose and protect the bud.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What does a seed contain?
questions.explanation: A seed has an embryo, which is the baby plant, and food stored for it.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Seeds inside fleshy, sweet fruits are mostly dispersed by:
options: Animals and birds that eat the fruit
questions.explanation: Animals eat the fruit and drop the seeds elsewhere.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of the following can carry pollen from one flower to another?
options: Bees and other insects, wind and birds
questions.explanation: Insects, wind, birds and water can all carry pollen.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Name three conditions needed for a seed to germinate.
questions.answer: A seed needs water, air (oxygen) and a suitable temperature to germinate.
keyPoints: Water
Air or oxygen
Suitable temperature
questions.explanation: Light is not needed for most seeds to germinate.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Sugarcane is grown from pieces of stem. What must each piece have to grow into a new plant?
questions.explanation: New shoots and roots arise from the buds at the nodes.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Maize flowers are small and have no bright colour or scent. How are they pollinated?
questions.answer: They are pollinated by wind. Wind carries the light pollen from one flower to another, so showy petals and scent are not needed to attract insects.
keyPoints: Wind pollination
No need to attract insects
questions.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers usually make a lot of light pollen.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many seconds are there in one hour?
questions.explanation: 1 hour = 60 minutes = 60 x 60 = 3600 seconds.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The motion of a child on a swing is an example of:
questions.explanation: A swing repeats its to-and-fro motion at regular intervals.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How does the time period of a simple pendulum change when its length is increased?
questions.explanation: A longer pendulum takes more time for each oscillation.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these is an example of circular motion?
options: A stone tied to a string and whirled in a circle
A car moving on a straight road
A book lying on a table
questions.explanation: The stone moves along a circular path.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is an oscillation? Give an example.
questions.answer: An oscillation is a complete to-and-fro movement about a fixed position, such as the bob of a simple pendulum swinging from one side to the other and back.
keyPoints: To-and-fro movement
A correct example such as a pendulum
questions.explanation: Periodic to-and-fro motion is called oscillatory motion.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is a speed of 36 km/h in metres per second?

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Car A covers 100 km in 2 hours and car B covers 150 km in 3 hours, each at a steady speed. Which car is faster?
questions.answer: Speed of A = 100 / 2 = 50 km/h. Speed of B = 150 / 3 = 50 km/h. Both cars have the same speed.
keyPoints: Speed of A is 50 km/h
Speed of B is 50 km/h so neither is faster
questions.explanation: Speeds must be calculated before comparing them.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The glowing of the filament of an electric bulb is due to which effect of current?
questions.explanation: The filament gets so hot that it glows.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these is needed to make a simple electric circuit glow a bulb?
options: A cell, wires and a bulb joined in a closed loop
questions.explanation: A closed loop with a source and a bulb is needed.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which is a use of an electromagnet?
options: Lifting heavy iron scrap in a crane
questions.explanation: Strong electromagnets in cranes lift and drop iron scrap.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The direction of electric current, as normally shown in circuit diagrams, is from:
options: The negative terminal to the positive terminal of the cell through the circuit
The positive terminal to the negative terminal of the cell through the circuit
questions.explanation: By convention, current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal outside the cell.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: List the components of a simple electric circuit.
questions.answer: A simple circuit has a source of electricity such as a cell or battery, connecting wires, a device such as a bulb, and a switch to open or close the circuit.
keyPoints: Cell or battery and wires
Bulb or other device and switch
questions.explanation: These parts make a complete path for the current.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: An electromagnet is made from an iron nail wrapped with insulated wire. What happens when the current in the wire is switched off?
options: The nail stays a strong magnet
questions.explanation: An electromagnet is a temporary magnet that works only while current flows.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What could happen if a thick copper wire is used instead of a proper fuse wire?
questions.answer: A copper wire does not melt easily, so it would not cut off the circuit when the current becomes too large. The appliances and wires could overheat, be damaged or start a fire.
keyPoints: Copper wire will not melt readily
Circuit is not cut off, so overheating or fire may occur
questions.explanation: A fuse must melt first to protect the circuit.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What type of reflection takes place from a smooth, shiny surface such as a mirror?
questions.explanation: A smooth surface reflects parallel rays in one direction, giving regular reflection.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which instrument is used in a submarine to see objects above the water?
questions.explanation: A periscope uses mirrors to look over an obstacle.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A disc painted with the seven colours of the rainbow is rotated very fast. How does it appear?
questions.explanation: The colours blend in the eye to give a whitish appearance, as in Newton's colour disc.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: As an object is moved closer to a light source, the size of its shadow:
questions.explanation: A nearer object blocks a wider cone of light, so the shadow grows.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How does a simple periscope work?
questions.answer: A periscope has two plane mirrors fixed at 45 degrees to the tube, one at each end. Light from the object is reflected from the upper mirror to the lower mirror and then to the eye.
keyPoints: Two plane mirrors at 45 degrees
Light is reflected twice into the eye
questions.explanation: Reflection from two mirrors lets us see over or around obstacles.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which word looks exactly the same when its image is seen in a plane mirror held to the side of the word (a vertical mirror)?
questions.explanation: M and O are symmetrical about a vertical line, so MOM reads the same in the mirror.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: We can see our image clearly in a still pond but not on a wooden table. Explain.
questions.answer: The surface of still water is smooth and acts like a mirror, giving regular reflection that forms a clear image. A wooden table is rough, so it scatters light in many directions and no clear image forms.
keyPoints: Smooth surface gives regular reflection
Rough surface scatters light
questions.explanation: Clear images need regular reflection from a smooth surface.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which part of a plant mainly absorbs water from the soil?
questions.explanation: Roots, with their root hairs, absorb water and minerals.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The sundew is a plant that gets part of its nutrition by:
questions.explanation: Sundew is an insectivorous plant.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A lichen is made of which two organisms living together?
questions.explanation: In a lichen an alga and a fungus live in a symbiotic relationship.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Urea, used in agriculture as a fertiliser, mainly supplies which nutrient to plants?
questions.explanation: Urea is rich in nitrogen.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is a leaf boiled in alcohol before it is tested with iodine solution?
questions.answer: Boiling in alcohol removes the green chlorophyll from the leaf. The leaf becomes pale so that any blue-black colour from starch can be seen clearly.
keyPoints: Alcohol removes chlorophyll
The colour change can then be seen clearly
questions.explanation: Without removing the green colour, the iodine test result would be hard to see.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The leaves of a wheat crop turn yellowish though water and sunlight are plentiful. Which nutrient shortage is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is needed for making chlorophyll and proteins, and its shortage turns leaves pale.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Compare the way a green plant and a cow obtain their food.
questions.answer: A green plant is an autotroph and makes its own food by photosynthesis using sunlight. A cow is a heterotroph and depends on plants for ready-made food, which it digests in its alimentary canal.
keyPoints: Plant makes its own food by photosynthesis
Cow depends on other organisms for food
questions.explanation: Autotrophs make food while heterotrophs depend on others.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the process of taking food into the body called?
questions.explanation: Ingestion is taking in food.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which is the largest gland in the human body?
questions.explanation: The liver is the largest gland.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Saliva changes the starch in food into:
questions.explanation: An enzyme in saliva breaks starch down to sugar, so bread tastes sweet if chewed for long.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which opening ends the alimentary canal?
questions.explanation: Undigested waste leaves the body through the anus.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is it advised to chew food well before swallowing?
questions.answer: Chewing breaks the food into small pieces and mixes it with saliva. This makes it easier for the digestive juices to act on it.
keyPoints: Food broken into small pieces
Mixes with saliva so that digestion is easier
questions.explanation: Digestion starts in the mouth.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: If the villi of the small intestine were damaged, which function would be most affected?
questions.explanation: Villi provide the large surface area for absorbing digested food.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does absorbed food have to reach the blood?
questions.answer: The blood carries the absorbed food to all parts of the body. The cells use it to obtain energy, to grow and to repair themselves.
keyPoints: Blood carries food to all cells
Cells use it for energy, growth and repair
questions.explanation: Blood transport links digestion to the cells.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these animals gives wool?
questions.explanation: Goats such as the angora and Kashmiri goat give wool.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the larva of the silk moth called?
questions.explanation: The caterpillar of the silk moth is called the silkworm.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Inside the cocoon, the silk moth is in which stage?
questions.explanation: The larva changes into a pupa inside the cocoon.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: After the burrs are removed, which steps change the cleaned wool fibres into yarn?
questions.explanation: The fibres are dyed and then spun into yarn.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why are silk cocoons put in hot water or steam in the process of getting silk?
questions.answer: The hot water or steam softens the sticky substance that holds the threads together. The silk threads can then be unwound from the cocoon.
keyPoints: Softens the sticky material
Allows threads to be unwound (reeled)
questions.explanation: Reeling needs the cocoon threads to be loosened.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which pair correctly matches an animal with the fibre it gives?
questions.explanation: Silkworms give silk, while yaks and sheep give wool.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A student says that silk threads are made by the adult silk moth. Correct the statement.
questions.answer: Silk threads are made by the larva (silkworm), which spins a cocoon around itself. The adult moth does not make silk.
keyPoints: Larva spins the cocoon
Adult moth does not make silk
questions.explanation: The cocoon is spun in the larval stage.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which instrument is used to measure the body temperature of a person?
questions.explanation: A clinical thermometer is made for body temperature.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What does temperature tell us about an object?
options: How hot or cold it is
questions.explanation: Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: One end of an iron rod is held in a flame. After some time the other end becomes hot. Heat travelled along the rod by:
questions.explanation: Heat is conducted along a solid from the hot end to the cold end.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A room heater warms the air of a whole room mainly through:
questions.explanation: Warm air rises and cooler air moves in, setting up convection currents.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is radiation? Give an example from daily life.
questions.answer: Radiation is the transfer of heat without any medium, in the form of heat rays. We feel the warmth of the Sun or a fire even when no matter carries the heat to us.
keyPoints: Heat transfer without a medium
Example such as sunlight or a fire
questions.explanation: Radiation can travel through empty space.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: People in hot deserts often wear loose, light-coloured clothes. Why?
options: Light colours reflect heat and loose clothes let air move around the body
questions.explanation: Reflecting heat and allowing air to move keep the body cooler.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: An ice cube is held in the palm of the hand. In which direction does the heat flow, and why does the hand feel cold?
questions.answer: Heat flows from the warmer hand to the colder ice. The hand loses heat to the ice, so it feels cold while the ice melts.
keyPoints: Heat flows from hand to ice
Hand loses heat so it feels cold
questions.explanation: Heat always goes from a hotter to a colder body.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which acid is present in our stomach and helps in digestion?
questions.explanation: The stomach makes dilute hydrochloric acid.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these is a base?
questions.explanation: Slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) is a base.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which solution has no effect on either red or blue litmus paper?
questions.explanation: Sugar solution is neutral.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: When vinegar is added to baking soda, bubbles of which gas are produced?
questions.explanation: An acid and baking soda give out carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Give two examples each of acidic and basic substances found at home.
questions.answer: Acidic: vinegar and lemon juice. Basic: baking soda and soap solution.
keyPoints: Two correct acids such as vinegar and lemon juice
Two correct bases such as baking soda and soap
questions.explanation: Foods that are sour are acidic, and soaps and many cleaners are basic.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Soap solution turns turmeric red. A few drops of lemon juice are then added drop by drop. What is the most likely result?
options: The colour slowly returns to yellow as the base is neutralised
questions.explanation: The acid neutralises the base, so turmeric goes back to its yellow colour.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is lemon juice not a good remedy for an ant bite, while calamine solution is?
questions.answer: An ant bite contains formic acid. Lemon juice is also an acid and would not neutralise it, whereas calamine solution is a base and neutralises the acid.
keyPoints: Ant bite has formic acid
Only a base can neutralise it
questions.explanation: Neutralisation needs a base, not another acid.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Folding a sheet of paper into a boat is:
questions.explanation: Only the shape changes.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which gas of the air is needed for burning?
questions.explanation: Burning needs oxygen.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Souring of milk and its change into curd is:
questions.explanation: New substances such as lactic acid are formed.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: When a hot saturated solution of a salt cools and crystals form, the change is:
questions.explanation: The same substance is obtained as crystals, so no new substance forms.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is galvanisation and why is it done?
questions.answer: Galvanisation is the process of coating iron with a thin layer of zinc. It protects the iron from rusting because it keeps air and water from the iron.
keyPoints: Coating of iron with zinc
Prevents rusting
questions.explanation: Galvanised pipes and sheets last much longer.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A student dissolves salt in water and then fries an egg. Which statement is correct?
options: Dissolving is physical and frying is chemical
Dissolving is chemical and frying is physical
questions.explanation: Salt can be recovered by evaporating the water, but a fried egg cannot become raw again.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A magnesium ribbon is burnt and the white ash is dissolved in water. What does the solution do to red litmus paper, and what does this show?
questions.answer: The solution turns red litmus blue. This shows that magnesium oxide dissolves in water to form a base, so burning magnesium has formed a new substance.
keyPoints: Red litmus turns blue
A new substance, a base, has formed
questions.explanation: A new substance with different properties shows a chemical change.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which animal of the desert has a hump on its back?
questions.explanation: The camel is adapted to the desert and its hump stores fat.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In which unit is rainfall usually measured?
questions.explanation: Rainfall is measured as the depth of water, in millimetres.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How does the hump of a camel help it in the desert?
options: It stores fat that can be used when food is scarce
questions.explanation: Fat in the hump is a store of energy for long periods without food.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: When the air is very humid, it contains:
questions.explanation: Humid air is moist.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Name two elements of weather and the instrument used to measure each.
questions.answer: Temperature is measured with a thermometer, and rainfall is measured with a rain gauge. Wind speed is measured with an anemometer.
keyPoints: Temperature with a thermometer
Rainfall with a rain gauge or another correct pair
questions.explanation: Different instruments measure different elements of weather.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: 'The summers in Rajasthan are generally hot and dry.' This statement describes:
questions.explanation: It describes the usual pattern over many years.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why do some animals of very cold regions migrate to warmer places or hibernate in winter?
questions.answer: In winter food is scarce and the cold is severe. Migrating to a warmer place or hibernating in a sheltered place helps the animal to survive the harsh season.
keyPoints: Scarce food and severe cold
Migration or hibernation helps survival
questions.explanation: These habits are adaptations to seasonal changes.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A thunderstorm is usually accompanied by:
questions.explanation: Thunderstorms bring lightning, thunder, heavy rain and gusty winds.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why are cyclone shelters built along the coast?
options: To protect people from the effects of a cyclone
questions.explanation: They provide a safe place during a cyclone.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Around the eye of a cyclone, the winds:
questions.explanation: The winds whirl in a spiral around the low-pressure centre.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Air exerts pressure:
questions.explanation: Air pressure acts in all directions.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is a tornado?
questions.answer: A tornado is a violently spinning, funnel-shaped column of air that extends from a thunderstorm cloud to the ground. It can cause great damage along its path.
keyPoints: Funnel-shaped spinning column of air
Extends from cloud to the ground
questions.explanation: Tornadoes are small but very destructive storms.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: At the centre of a cyclone the air pressure is:
questions.explanation: A cyclone is a system of low pressure, so air rushes in towards its centre.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A student says that trees move and so wind is made. Correct the idea.
questions.answer: Trees sway because wind is blowing; they do not cause it. Wind is caused by differences in air pressure produced by uneven heating of the Earth by the Sun.
keyPoints: Swaying of trees is an effect of wind
Wind is due to uneven heating and pressure differences
questions.explanation: Cause and effect should not be mixed up.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Compared with the air we breathe in, the air we breathe out has more:
questions.explanation: Exhaled air has more carbon dioxide than inhaled air.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the purpose of respiration in living things?
questions.explanation: Respiration releases the energy stored in food.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which food substance is broken down in cells to release energy in respiration?
questions.explanation: Glucose is the main fuel for cellular respiration.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How does the breathing rate of a person who is running compare with that when resting?
questions.explanation: More energy is needed, so breathing is faster.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the role of the diaphragm in breathing?
questions.answer: The diaphragm is a muscular sheet below the lungs. When it moves down the chest cavity enlarges and air enters; when it moves up the cavity gets smaller and air leaves.
keyPoints: Muscular sheet below the lungs
Moves down for inhalation and up for exhalation
questions.explanation: Movement of the diaphragm and ribs changes the space in the chest.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why is aerobic respiration more useful to the body than anaerobic respiration?
options: It releases much more energy from the same amount of glucose
questions.explanation: Complete breakdown of glucose with oxygen gives much more energy.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why do we feel warm after running or playing hard?
questions.answer: In respiration the cells release energy from food, and part of this energy appears as heat. More respiration during hard exercise means more heat is produced.
keyPoints: Respiration releases energy
Part of the energy is released as heat
questions.explanation: Respiration is how body heat is produced.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many kidneys does a normal human being have?
questions.explanation: Humans have a pair of kidneys.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which are the most numerous blood cells?
questions.explanation: Red blood cells are far more numerous than the others.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is the main function of red blood cells?
questions.explanation: Their haemoglobin carries oxygen.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How do plants absorb water from the soil?
questions.answer: Root hairs have thin walls and a large surface area. Water from the soil enters them and then passes to the xylem, which carries it up to the leaves.
keyPoints: Root hairs absorb water
Xylem carries it upward
questions.explanation: Root hairs are tiny extensions of root cells.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A potted plant that is not watered for many days starts to wilt. What is the best explanation?
options: The plant has too much food
Water is not available to be carried to the leaves and cells
The roots have too much sunlight
questions.explanation: Without water the plant cannot transport it, and the cells lose firmness.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Why does a plant lose more water by transpiration on a hot, dry day?
questions.answer: Heat and dry air make water evaporate faster from the leaves through the stomata. So the plant loses water more quickly on such a day.
keyPoints: Faster evaporation of water from leaves
Water is lost through stomata
questions.explanation: Transpiration rises with temperature and dryness.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these plants reproduces by spores?
questions.explanation: Mosses and ferns reproduce by spores.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which part of a plant produces seeds?
questions.explanation: Seeds develop in the flower after fertilisation.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these has unisexual flowers?
questions.explanation: Papaya has separate male and female flowers.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which of these has bisexual flowers, having both stamens and pistil?
questions.explanation: Mustard flowers have both male and female parts.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: What is budding? Name one organism that reproduces by it.
questions.answer: In budding, a small outgrowth called a bud forms on the parent, grows, and then separates to become a new organism. Yeast reproduces by budding.
keyPoints: Bud grows on the parent and separates
Example such as yeast
questions.explanation: Budding is a kind of asexual reproduction.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: After pollination, how does the male gamete reach the ovule?
options: Through a pollen tube that grows down the style
questions.explanation: The pollen grain grows a tube down the style to the ovule.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The seeds of a dandelion are very light and have fine hairs. How does this help the plant?
questions.answer: The light, hairy seeds float in the air and are carried far by the wind. This spreads the plant to new places.
keyPoints: Light and hairy seeds float in air
Wind carries them far away
questions.explanation: Such seeds are suited for dispersal by wind.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: How many metres are there in one kilometre?

questions.subject: science
questions.q: The hands of a clock move along a:
questions.explanation: The tips of the hands trace circles.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which expression gives the time taken to cover a distance at a steady speed?
questions.explanation: Time = distance / speed.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A modern wristwatch usually keeps time with the help of:
questions.explanation: Quartz clocks use a vibrating quartz crystal.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Convert 5 minutes into seconds.
questions.answer: 1 minute = 60 seconds, so 5 minutes = 5 x 60 = 300 seconds.
keyPoints: 1 minute is 60 seconds
The answer is 300 s
questions.explanation: Multiply minutes by 60 to get seconds.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: On a distance-time graph, one object has a steeper line than another. What does this mean?
questions.explanation: A steeper line means more distance in the same time.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: A train leaves at 8:00 am and reaches a town 150 km away at 10:30 am. Find its average speed.
questions.answer: Time taken = 2.5 hours. Average speed = 150 / 2.5 = 60 km/h.
keyPoints: Time taken is 2.5 hours
Speed is 60 km/h
questions.explanation: Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which metal is most commonly used for electrical connecting wires?
questions.explanation: Copper is a good and economical conductor.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: In an electric cell, which form of energy is converted into electrical energy?
questions.explanation: A cell has chemical substances that provide electrical energy.

questions.subject: science
questions.q: Which instrument can be used to detect the magnetic effect of current?
questions.explanation: A compass needle deflects near a wire carrying current.
